section_summaries.epidemiology: Malaria affects about 3 billion people globally, with 216 million cases and 445,000 deaths in 2016, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa. P. vivax accounts for 4% of global cases, rising to 41% outside Africa. Control efforts over the last two decades have reduced malaria mortality by 57%. Transmission is primarily through infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, but can also occur via blood transfusion or contaminated needles. Transmission intensity is influenced by vector abundance, longevity, temperature (optimal 20-30°C), rainfall, humidity, and proximity of human habitation to breeding sites. Changing conditions, such as irrigation schemes and new water reservoirs, can alter stable transmission patterns. The burden of severe disease has shifted from younger to older populations in some areas, and school-aged children are a significant reservoir for transmission.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Pathophysiological changes in malaria are mainly caused by blood-stage parasites, while exoerythrocytic stages, gametocytes, and sporozoites do not induce such changes. Infection begins with sporozoites invading hepatocytes, where asexual replication occurs asymptomatically. Merozoites are then released into the bloodstream, invading erythrocytes. P. falciparum and P. knowlesi can invade erythrocytes of any age, while P. vivax and P. ovale prefer younger cells and P. malariae prefers senescent ones. P. falciparum is unique due to sequestration, where late-stage parasitized erythrocytes bind to vascular endothelial cells in capillaries and venules of various organs, compromising blood flow. Fever is thought to result from schizont rupture. Anemia is caused by hemolysis, splenic clearance of infected RBCs, immune-mediated destruction of uninfected cells, bone marrow suppression, and dyserythropoiesis. Hypoglycemia results from parasite glucose consumption and inadequate hepatic gluconeogenesis, and can also be precipitated by antimalarial treatment. Metabolic acidosis is a significant marker of severity, often improving with effective IV treatment. Acute respiratory distress and acute kidney injury (more common in adults) are also observed, with renal failure linked to acute tubular necrosis and intravascular hemolysis.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Uncomplicated malaria typically presents as a non-specific febrile illness with headache, chills, rigors, anemia, and splenomegaly. Prodromal symptoms like malaise, myalgia, and mild fever may precede acute paroxysms. Periodic fevers, such as tertian (every 48 hours for P. vivax/falciparum) or quartan (every 72 hours for P. malariae), develop after several days. In endemic areas, older children and adults often acquire immunity, leading to asymptomatic parasitemia or milder illness. Non-immune individuals (e.g., young children, travelers) are at higher risk for severe and complicated malaria, which is a medical emergency. Complicated malaria can include cerebral malaria (coma, convulsions), severe anemia, metabolic acidosis, acute respiratory distress, acute kidney injury, and algid malaria (septic shock-like presentation). Clinical features vary between adults and children; cerebral malaria is more characteristic of pediatric severe malaria, while multi-organ involvement is frequent in adults. Post-malaria neurologic syndrome is a rare, transient complication.
section_summaries.diagnosis: The diagnosis of malaria infection must be confirmed parasitologically by visualizing parasites microscopically on a peripheral blood smear, detecting parasite antigens with a rapid diagnostic test (RDT), or by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Light microscopy, using thick and thin blood films, is considered the "gold standard"; thick films are superior for detecting parasites, while thin films are better for species identification and parasite morphology. RDTs are antigen-based dipstick or cassette tests that are simple to use and do not require electricity, though their performance varies in species differentiation and ability to distinguish new from recent infections. The choice of diagnostic method depends on the clinical context and available resources. Malarial retinopathy, observed via ocular funduscopic examination, is a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic sign for "true" cerebral malaria. Differential diagnosis for uncomplicated malaria is broad and includes viral syndromes, bacterial pneumonia, meningitis, dengue, leptospirosis, typhus, and viral hemorrhagic fevers.
section_summaries.treatment: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are the first-line treatment for all malarial infections, recommended by WHO to combat drug resistance. For uncomplicated falciparum malaria, five oral ACTs are recommended (e.g., artemether + lumefantrine) for a 3-day course, with primaquine often added in low-transmission areas to reduce transmission. Chloroquine is the recommended treatment for chloroquine-sensitive P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae; however, chloroquine-resistant P. vivax (e.g., in Indonesia and Papua New Guinea) requires ACTs. Radical cure for liver-stage P. vivax and P. ovale requires a second drug, such as tafenoquine or primaquine, after screening for G6PD deficiency. Severe malaria requires parenteral anti-malarials for at least 24 hours, followed by oral ACTs. IV artesunate is the first-line treatment for complicated malaria, with IM artemether as second-line. Supportive care includes monitoring vital signs, blood glucose, and addressing complications like hypoglycemia, acidosis, seizures, severe anemia, pulmonary edema, and renal failure.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention strategies include intermittent preventive treatment during pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP), recommended for pregnant women in malaria-endemic areas during the second trimester and onward. Intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi) with SP is also recommended in medium-to-high transmission areas, aligning with scheduled vaccine visits, provided parasite resistance is below 50%. Seasonal malarial chemoprevention (SMC) using amodiaquine and SP is advised for children under 6 in areas with short transmission seasons, like the Sahel. Additionally, significant efforts are underway to develop malaria vaccines. Pre-erythrocytic vaccines, like RTS,S (based on circumsporozoite protein), target the sporozoite/liver stage and have shown moderate efficacy. Blood-stage vaccines aim to reduce clinical severity, while transmission-blocking vaccines target mosquito-stage antigens to prevent parasite development in the vector.
